title: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?
desc: I saw this LinkedIn post from a Meta engineer and it resonated with me:https://www.linkedin.com/posts/ali-hamie_im-an-engineer-at-m...> I'm an engineer at Meta and I never felt this uncomfortable doin
content:
Hacker News new | past | comments | ask | show | jobs | submit login

Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don t understand?

251 points by rzk 9 hours ago | hide | past | favorite | 396 comments

I saw this LinkedIn post from a Meta engineer and it resonated with me: https: www.linkedin.com posts ali-hamie_im-an-engineer-at-m... I m an engineer at Meta and I never felt this uncomfortable doing my job. I m writing code these days and it all feels like a black box. This new standard of shipping with AI is moving so fast that if we re going to spend our time checking each line of code, it s going to take forever. That means you can end up with systems you ve built where you don t truly understand how all the code works. You understand the high level, but not every detail. And maybe this is becoming the new standard. It goes against every instinct of being a software engineer. I m used to understanding what I m building. Now I m trying to figure out how much I need to understand before I m comfortable moving forward. Are other engineers feeling this too? How are you handling this?

help

bitwizeshift 5 hours ago | next [–]

I’m surprised I haven’t see anyone say this yet, but I don’t let the LLM design the code at all, I let it implement a design I have created. By that I mean that, rather than let the LLM do the entire structure, I take the time to create the full hierarchy of abstractions and actors that I want my code to do. I decide, at the UML level, how abstractions will sit and interact — and then I make the LLM implement those gaps. The key thing here is that, by doing this, I DO know how the code works. I may not know how each unit is implemented, but I know each unit’s responsibilities and how they interact with one another. I’ve found that LLMs are HORRIBLE at writing decent abstractions, regardless of how much prompting and skills I’ve given it. It will always get the job done, but it will often be unmaintainable and require bigger and heavier refactors as I introduce more and more requirement changes. But by flexing my basic design skills, I don’t have those issues. Future refactoring fit into easy abstractions that I’ve designed. And by documenting it up front, I also have what becomes a living document on how this work will turn out. It takes a few hours up front to plan ahead, but it makes the LLMs job easier and use less tokens, and it makes the code better long term. I don’t care if one unit is suboptimal, as long as the abstraction is right — because at worst I can change an implementation for a better one later.

reply

fasterik 4 hours ago | parent | next [–]

I agree with this approach, but I m a bit surprised this has to be said at all. These are basic software design principles and I imagine it s the default way any experienced programmer would approach the problem. I wonder if the people not using this approach are primarily junior developers who have never seen how real software is built, or if it s leaking

whatsapp-mcp

Let your AI agent read your WhatsApp messages.

This is a small server that runs in your own Cloudflare account. You link your phone to it once, the way you'd link WhatsApp Web, and from then on any MCP client (Claude Code, Claude Desktop, anything that speaks MCP) can search and read your chats. It can read and search your messages, and remember names you give it for phone numbers. It can't send anything.

Ask your agent things like:

"What did Dana say about the flights?"

"Find every message where someone mentioned the lease, across all my chats."

"Summarize what I missed in the family group this week."

How it works

Your phone stays the source of truth. The server is a linked device that your agent talks to.

It doesn't stay connected to WhatsApp. When your agent asks for something, and once a day, it connects, collects whatever WhatsApp queued for it since last time, writes that to its own database, and hangs up. Your phone keeps working normally and keeps getting notifications.

Your messages live in a SQLite database inside a Durable Object in your Cloudflare account. Nothing goes anywhere else.

Set it up

You need a Cloudflare account on the Workers Paid plan (see the note below), Node 20 or later, and your phone.

git clone https://github.com/finereli/whatsapp-mcp
cd whatsapp-mcp
npm install

# 1. A place for the sign-in tokens. Paste the id it prints into wrangler.jsonc.
npx wrangler kv namespace create OAUTH_KV

# 2. A password for the page that links your phone. 12+ characters.
npx wrangler secret put OWNER_PASSWORD

# 3. Deploy.
npm run deploy

Wrangler prints your URL, something like https://whatsapp-mcp.your-name.workers.dev . Open it. The front page has the two remaining steps:

Link WhatsApp. Scan the QR code with WhatsApp (Settings, Linked Devices, Link a Device). If you're on the phone itself and can't scan a screen, use the phone number option instead. The first link imports your history. The page shows progress, and you can close it.

Connect your agent. In Claude Code:

claude mcp add --transport http whatsapp https://your-url/mcp

Then type /mcp and sign in with the password. Other clients: point t

title: If you don't run your own LLM proxy, how do you know whats going on?
desc:
Article URL: https://jrdsgl.com/if-you-dont-run-your-own-llm-proxy-how-the-fuck-do-you-even-know-whats-going-on/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50145507
Points: 3
# Comments: 1
content:
Menu

I think the title captures the idea fully but I'll dig into it because this ain't Twitter.

You're working an idea, a piece of code, or a multibillion a year SaaS app which is probably saving the world. Maybe you're automating the cloning process of grabbing new Labubu release images and taking the 2D image and using a ComfyUI to translate it into a 3D CAD to get the replica production started faster because CNY is on the horizon and global manufacturing halts around that time. Maybe you like to use your tokens to search against the most powerful computer software ever developed for macronutrient information for a McRib or some shit.

You're most likely chatting with some type of frontend thats tied into a paid subscription from the provider of your choice. TUI, GUI, Voice call, whatever. It's your data going in and their data coming back for you. That's what they're selling, I'm happy to buy that right now. They'll show you something like this as proof of work happening:

yikes y'all

That is a distraction. That is not token usage statistics with time series data meant for engineers. I can't make a decision with this bullshit. Surely the big labs will have valuable insight to share with the curious user who digs into the Analytics panel.

I can't make a decision with this bullshit. I hear you already, "there's OTel export options!!1!". Cool, I guess. This is one reason, here's 5 more off of the top of my head right now:

multi provider, multi models, at a single endpoint you control

logs of which key called what model with what client at what time and its status

use virtual api keys to stop littering your single main key over your work, agents, and harnesses

its infra you control

you can pivot model and provider extremely fast without resetting everything up (again, probably, for like the 3rd time)

I'm not going to suggest a proxy provider for you to use, only that you run it yourself somewhere you control. When you pick one, don't forget you can modify it for your actual needs. I've modded mine for better insight, for custom MCP server endpoints, additional features. Whatever you choose, you should be getting something along these lines for data.

When I see a cache miss during a coding session, I can pinpoint why that happened in 20 seconds by hand. I haven't automated it but the proxy I use has an API, so it's possible to automate.

Own your infrastructure, your application visibility, data pathing, and storage. I do this at home because it's fun and it's how I like to learn. I do this at work because I'm not doing my job right if I don't. I may never fully understand how the fuck a large language model works well enough to white board it in an interview. But I can wrassle it down and make sure it's instrumented while serving inference.

Don t make me use your harness

I cancelled my Claude subscription today because I can t use

Title: Hybrid Reasoning Agents

Authors: Jiaru Zou , Yunzhe Qi , Sirui Chen , Federico Bianchi , Shang Zhu , Pan Lu , Jingrui He , James Zou

View a PDF of the paper titled Hybrid Reasoning Agents, by Jiaru Zou and 7 other authors

View PDF
HTML (experimental)

Abstract: How can we build an agent that thinks beyond human language, yet still acts through it in the external environment? Modern LLM agents still reason and interact through text, while latent reasoning offers an efficient internal medium but lacks native tool access and reasoning transparency. We bridge these two directions with Hybrid Reasoning Agents (HybridAgents), which dynamically navigate between latent reasoning and text-based interaction throughout a unified generation process. Architecturally, a lightweight HybridLink enables seamless transitions between text and latent modes, while the agent s continuous working memory preserves lossless hybrid context across multiple turns. These designs preserve tool-integrated agentic capabilities while making latent thoughts directly inspectable. Building on this architecture, we further develop dedicated post-training algorithms for hybrid reasoning: HybridSFT stabilizes tool-integrated hybrid generation by teaching the backbone to coordinate with HybridLink, then HybridRL scales reasoning by learning when to think in latent space and when to act through text. We evaluate HybridAgent at 3 model scales across 11 benchmarks covering mathematics, science, medicine, search, and agentic reasoning. Compared with frontier LLM Agents and agentic frameworks spanning both text-based and latent methods, HybridAgent consistently improves performance by 10.4%, while delivering 35.5%-54.7% token reduction, 1.8x-2.6x faster inference, and 2.7x-3.7x cost savings. Code and data are available at this https URL .

content:
Skip to main content

Search / Fetch API is now available, powered by our in-house search engine and supporting web search and fetch. Click here to view the guide.

On this page

Search Fetch

The Search API and the Fetch API give agents and RAG applications access to live web content:

Search API finds web pages for a query and returns structured results. It is powered by DeepSeek s in-house search engine.

Fetch API retrieves a single web page and returns its content as Markdown.

Both are raw JSON APIs. They use the same bearer authentication as the DeepSeek API.

The base URL is https://api.deepseek.com :

API Endpoint

Search POST https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search

Fetch POST https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/fetch

See the Search API Reference and Fetch API Reference for the complete request and response schemas.

Authentication ​

Send your API key and the JSON content type in the request headers:

Header Required Value

Authorization Yes Bearer DeepSeek API Key

Content-Type Yes application/json

Search API ​

Request ​

curl https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search \
-H Authorization: Bearer DeepSeek API Key \
-H Content-Type: application/json \
-d {
query : DeepSeek V4 release ,
count : 5,
need_content : true
}

import requests

response = requests . post (
https://api.deepseek.com/v1/tools/search ,
headers = {
Authorization : Bearer DeepSeek API Key ,
} ,
json = {
query : DeepSeek V4 release ,
count : 5 ,
need_content : True ,
} ,
)
response . raise_for_status ( )

for result in response . json ( ) [ results ] :
print ( result [ title ] , result [ url ] )
print ( result [ summary ] )

Request fields:

Field Type Required Default Description

query string Yes - The search query must contain 1 to 128 Unicode characters, cannot be all whitespace, and supports the query operators listed below.

count integer No 10 The number of results to return, between 1 and 50.

ori_question string No - The user s original question that triggered the search, between 1 and 128 characters, to improve query understanding, with null treated as not provided.

localization string No An optional IP address used to localize search results.

need_content boolean No false Whether to return page content in content , which is always an empty string when false .

Unknown fields in the request body are ignored.

Query Operators ​

The query is forwarded with its search syntax intact. The examples below combine operators with a search term; you can combine multiple operators in one query.

Operator Example Description

site: DeepSeek site:github.com Restrict results to the given site, and to target multiple sites, separate the site: clauses with spaces and join them with OR , for example DeepSeek site:github.com OR site:huggingface.co .

-site: DeepSeek -site:example.com Exclude the given site, and separate multiple sites with spaces.

- DeepSeek -advertisement Exclude pages containing the term, and separate multiple terms with spaces.

- ... DeepSeek - release

Anthropic says it’s committing 5% of its shares to a ‘public benefit fund’

Anthropic announced today that it’s creating a “public benefit fund” that will give the company “increased flexibility and scale” to support projects for societal good.

Anthropic said that it will commit 5% of its shares to the fund — structured as a wholly-owned entity within the company — with the option to contribute an additional 2% for every 50% increase in Anthropic’s value. And it offered some broad-strokes ideas for how this money might actually be used, such as “large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.”

There s also the impact that AI might have on the job market, which Anthropic has already committed $200 million to study . But the company said, “Given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.”

Anthropic’s announcement comes as the AI industry faces increasingly negative public sentiment, which CEO Dario Amodei has described as “fundamentally a crisis of trust.”

If you’re wondering who will actually decide which public benefits are worth funding, Anthropic said it will share more information about structure and governance in the coming months.

Meta removes language that raised scraping and AI training concerns

Meta recently updated its commercial terms of use, declaring that the company can “use any content from [a business account’s] domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of” Meta products and services.

According to legal experts interviewed by Nieman Lab , this looked like a “remarkable provision” that could give Meta permission to scrape the website of any publisher with a Meta business account and use the content to train the company’s AI models. (While Meta defeated a high-profile lawsuit over alleged copyright infringement last year, other cases against AI companies, including Meta, continue.)

However, a Meta spokesperson insisted that the updated terms did not reflect a change in the way Meta crawls the web. And now, The Verge reports that the provision has been removed.

“We’ve heard you and want to clarify: the crawling terms we consolidated only applied to our ads and business products, and we’ve clarified that in the terms themselves,” the company said in a statement. “It does not change how Meta uses web crawlers.”

Anthropic says its workforce has become less junior and is spending more time in meetings

Anthony Ha

1:21 PM PDT · October 17, 2026

The composition of Anthropic’s workforce and the type of work getting done have changed significantly in the past year, according to a report that the AI company published on Friday.

Anthropic argues that its own workplace trends could be indicators of “how AI will shift work organization, hiring, and labor demand across the economy,” especially since the company “has thoroughly molded its workflows around AI.” But even if other organizations never embrace AI as thoroughly or in the exact same way as Anthropic, the report offers an intriguing glimpse at how the company currently operates.

Notably, Anthropic is making fewer junior hires, with the proportion of junior-level employees in technical departments falling from 21% to 14% since early 2025, and the proportion of junior technical hires falling even more sharply, from 27% to 9%.

Anthropic also says that technical teams now represent a smaller share of the overall workforce, falling from 61% to 56% — a trend that it attributes to “natural expansion of business functions as the company scales,” as well as “coding tools increasingly allowing non-technical employees to make software themselves.”

One employee reportedly described an “eternal pressure at Anthropic to move as fast as possible and use Claude for everything.” In an April 2026 survey, 27% of employees said they had become more productive because of Claude and 20% said their job had shifted “from actually doing work to managing Claudes”; apparently one engineered compared this to babysitting: “When you are babysitting, every child brings to you concerns with an equal demand for your attention and the various [Claudes] also do that.”

In fact, the report suggests “human attention and judgement” are becoming a “bottleneck” for productivity, as Claude produces a “deluge” of text that needs to be read and organized.

Unsurprisingly, the report argues that AI adoption has made the company more productive, as indicated by “more code per person, closing more sales per rep, and processing more contracts.” The company acknowledges that “more code does not necessarily mean better code or business impact,” but it also hasn’t found any indications that code quality is declining.

The report says that based on calendar data, meeting time per employee is up 20% compared to a year ago, and it s up 16% for technical contributors. The company attributes this to the importance of “human trust and accountability,” with employees repeatedly describing “face-to-face coordination as indispensable.”

FLUX 3 Image Klein

October 15, 2026 4 min read

Today we are releasing FLUX 3 Image Klein, a 5.6B parameter open weights model for text-to-image generation, image editing and multi-reference generation with up to 10 reference images. It shares core capabilities with the full FLUX 3 Image model: native 4K generation, pixel-perfect editing, and bounding boxes that control where elements are placed or confine edits to a defined area.

FLUX 3 Image Klein builds on FLUX 3 s shared learnings across images, video and audio. Images contribute spatial detail, video adds motion and physical dynamics, and audio provides information about events and interactions. Together, these signals help the model generate images that feel grounded in the real world.

The release includes a base model for fine-tuning and a step distilled model for low-latency generation, along with FP8, INT8 and NVFP4 builds developed with NVIDIA support, under the FLUX Kommunity License.

Try it in the BFL API · Download the weights

Leading open weights quality with fewer parameters

In internal evaluations, FLUX 3 Image Klein ranks first in text-to-image, multi-reference generation and image editing, ahead of larger open weights models. It also rates above the closed models in the comparison, Ideogram V4.5 and FLUX.2 [pro]. At 5.6B parameters, it is the smallest open model in the comparison, against 7B for Qwen-Image 2.1 and 12.9B for Krea 2. Compared with FLUX.2 [klein] 9B, it gains 91 Elo in text-to-image and 70 in image editing, with 38% fewer parameters.

Parameter counts are for the image generator, as each publisher reports them; text encoders are not counted. Krea 2 does not support image editing and is not included in the image editing comparison.

FLUX 3 Image Klein was also optimized for consumer GPUs. Fewer parameters make it practical to run locally and cheaper to adapt, and teams with data sovereignty or local deployment requirements can evaluate and adapt the model on their own infrastructure. This is also key for on-device image editing, allowing consumers to edit images directly on their favorite laptops. The generator weights require 11.2 GB in BF16 and 5.6 GB in FP8. With the INT8 build, FLUX 3 Image Klein runs on NVIDIA GeForce RTX GPUs with as little as 8GB of VRAM, through ComfyUI or Diffusers, extending what FLUX.2 [klein] started to even smaller hardware. With the distilled model and the INT8 build, it generates a 1MP image in about 4 seconds on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 5090 and under 9 seconds on an RTX 4070 through ComfyUI.

How do you review code at the volume agents produce it? On the Claude Code team, once we had high coverage and deep reviews, we started optimizing for the minimum amount of human review time that doesn t raise reverts or incidents.

We ve said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code s own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it?

This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code s codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent.

We didn t remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes.

RETHINKING THE PURPOSE OF CODE REVIEW

When agents write code, the number of changes goes up, fast. In Anthropic s monorepo, changes landing per day went from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September this year.

Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it s seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible.

Code review does two jobs:

Find and fix issues before they ship

Build shared context and codebase understanding across the team

This article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end.

We think did a human read the code? is an imprecise proxy for what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?

Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague.

Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny.

content:
You could have invented transformers from memory

Every layer is a memory store

[code] [interactive app]

Contents Retrieving a character from memory. The recall worsens as the number of memories grows. Large language models today can recall obscure facts from every corner of the world.
Most recently, I was running late for a friend s board game night, so I asked Astra to remind me the rules to Dune: Imperium.
It gladly narrated them to me as I drove over and helped me remember the rules well enough for me to play again.
We re so used to asking models about anything that we take their vast knowledge for granted.

How do models remember so much information? And how much can they store?

In this post, I ll go through an intuitive way to look at linear maps, MLPs, and self-attention as different kinds of memory stores. From this intuition we can derive some heuristics for how much memory each layer can store.

The key property that characterizes a good memory store is its ability to recall what it stored. After all, even if we could store infinitely many facts, it s not very helpful if we can t recall them when we need to.
The more memories we store, the more they interfere with each other when we try to recall one. So throughout the post we ll focus on one quantity, the interference-to-signal ratio, which measures how much the other memories get in the way during recall. The number of memories a store can hold before the interference grows as large as the signal is its capacity .

We ll develop this perspective and show how you can go from a linear layer to something better, an MLP, which improves both capacity and recall, and then all the way to self-attention, which has very good recall and can store a potentially unbounded number of memories. With 64-dimensional keys, that s a jump from about 64 memories, to about 2,700, to over a million.

Here are the terms we ll use throughout. A memory store is a function $f$ that holds $M$ memories, for $i = 1, \ldots, M$. A memory is one key-value pair: a key $k_i \in \reals^{d_k}$, used for lookup based on similarity, and a value $v_i \in \reals^{d_v}$, which is what we want to retrieve. To use $f$, we query it with an input $x$, and it recalls an output $f(x)$. A good memory store recalls $v_i$ when we query it with $k_i$, or with another vector similar to $k_i$. In the literature, a memory store that recalls by similarity is called an associative memory .

An outer product memory store #

The most basic memory store is linear: it simply accumulates memories via outer products,

$$W = \sum_{i=1}^{M} v_i k_i\transpose = V\transpose K$$ where the rows of $K \in \reals^{M\times d_k}$ and $V \in \reals^{M\times d_v}$ are the keys $k_i\transpose$ and the values $v_i\transpose$. 1

To store a new memory $(k, v)$, we simply add $vk\transpose$ to the existing weights. 2

Aside: a gradient descent step writes a memory Take a linear layer $y = Wx$ inside a network with a scalar loss $L$, and let $\bar y = \grad L

content:
Frontier Red Team

Claude reveals ECDSA curve origins

Oct 16, 2026

“It’s just timestamps”: the decades-old mystery of the origins of one of the most popular cryptographic standards has been explained.

We pursued this long-standing open question of the cryptographic community to settle concerns about ECDSA, which is one of our most widely used cryptographic standards.

Readers should take this as a fun closing chapter and the end of years of speculation. There is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Most researchers trusted the curves already. Enjoy.

ECDSA is the most widely used elliptic curve cryptography standard. It was adopted by NIST in 2000 as part of the FIPS 186-2 Digital Signature Standard which lists a set of standard elliptic curves of varying sizes and security levels. For curves over prime and binary fields, the specifications published a “seed” parameter whose hash value is used to define the coefficient b of the curve. The provenance of these seeds has been a long-standing question, as they were provided by the NSA with no explanation or justification. As an example, the NIST P-256 curve seed was SEED = C49D3608 86E70493 6A6678E1 139D26B7 819F7E90 with no information where it came from.

Neal Koblitz and Alfred Menezes wrote an excellent summary on this controversy, “ A Riddle Wrapped in an Enigma ”, which discusses the history and concerns around the seed values. This mystery led to an amateur investigation into the origin of the seeds and a bounty for anyone who could find them .

The best story was that Jerry Solinas, longtime NSA employee, generated the seeds using a hash of a humorous passphrase:

“I believe there was a counter rather than multiple hashing, but I don’t know details. The message was along the lines of ‘Give Bob and Jerry a raise’ or ‘Bob and Jerry rule’ or something like that. It was Bob Reiter who actually wrote the code, and he doesn’t remember the details either. Nor were we able to find archives from so long ago. If they exist, they are no doubt sitting on a hard drive near the Ark of the Covenant.”

Jerry Solinas, 2015

Unfortunately, Jerry died in 2023 and other colleagues at the time were not responsive, leaving open the question of how these seeds were originally derived.

Claude found the seeds

Several Anthropic employees had unsuccessfully chased the seeds following the tip about it being a hash of a humorous phrase. That turned out to be wrong. In October 2026, a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model if it could figure out how those seeds were generated without pointing at the clue.

In under half an hour , Claude discovered the origins of the NIST P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 seeds. None of them were the results of any hash algorithm at all, but rather the output of the C library’s lrand48 random-number generator, seeded with a Unix timestamp!

The algorithm used would sample bytes from the random number generator (RNG) initialized by a Unix timestamp

Muse Spark Open is available today and brings leading agentic capabilities to your desktop for the first time on Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios.

Today, we’re releasing the weights for Muse Spark Open, the most capable US open-weight model to date. Muse Spark Open is a natively multimodal model with 816B total parameters (42B active) and a 1M-token context window. Built for coding and agentic work, it excels at long-horizon tasks, complex software engineering, and multi-step reasoning.

We believe the future is for everyone , and that includes the freedom to run advanced models wherever, including at home. Muse Spark Open is the first model in its class to run on your desktop using two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios with the latest MLX framework.

Muse Spark Open is available today through API platforms at Baseten, Fireworks AI, Groq, Modal, Nebius, OpenRouter and Together AI. Model weights are available for download on Amazon SageMaker AI, Google Cloud Model Garden, Hugging Face, and Microsoft Foundry Models.

It runs on leading inference engines like SGLang, vLLM, TensorRT-LLM, Hugging Face Transformers, Apple MLX, llama.cpp, and Unsloth with optimizations for AMD, Apple, Intel, and NVIDIA silicon. Developers can easily further customize the model using the PyTorch framework.

Key Benchmarks

For more details about our evaluations, see the evaluation methodology report .

Optimized for Apple Silicon

Leveraging the latest version of MLX, Muse Spark Open was optimized to run on Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, and together they’re the best way to run a powerful model on your own desktop.

Apple’s unified memory architecture lets the M5 Ultra s integrated GPU use up to 512 GB per Mac Studio, so two machines can hold an entire model. And the chip’s 1.2 TB/s of memory bandwidth is fast enough to read the small slice each token needs. The result is two Mac Studios behave like one supercomputer with a terabyte of unified memory.

We tested a range of agentic workflows running entirely on-device, using Muse Code powered by Muse Spark Open, including shipping real iOS changes to Ice Cubes (an open-source Mastodon client) — bug fixes, new features, full build — and driving DaVinci Resolve end to end, with the model reviewing footage frame by frame to find the strongest moments and crop them vertically.

Available Now

We’re sharing this work because we want everyone to have access to the best models. The open-weight version of Muse Spark ships with custom, auto-tunable Helion GPU kernels in SGLang, delivering 1.03-3.95× kernel-level speedups on NVIDIA and AMD GPUs, and a 3% end-to-end speedup on AMD MI350.

Safety and Preparedness

After my mother passed away I ended up with a big box full of old film negatives containing photos from childhood family trips and similar. So I decided to buy a negative photo scanner and found that the Plustek 8200i was supported under Linux so I bought that. Only to discover that the chipset in the scanner had changed to one that wasn t supported under Linux anymore. So I had some success making Linux configuration tools for some of my hardware using Claude code, like my Dell Camera controller app so I thought, maybe Claude can help me get a working SANE driver. I basically got stuck and got nowhere for the longest time and even basically gave up on the project for a few Months.

Then I saw a post on X from Tom Crider aka Glorious Eggroll talking about how he had managed to fix a mouse driver using AI tooling. He basically described how he set it up so that the AI agent had full control of a Windows instance to capture data needed to fix the driver. So I pasted his tweet into Claude and asked it to help me set up a windows virtual machine to do the same things Tom as doing for my scanner. I think the combination of having the ability to run scans under windows and capture the USB data while doing so worked wonders, probably combined with improvements to Claude code made a huge difference. Within a few hours I had my first ever working scan under Linux, sure with some quality issues, but 100% recognizable as the image in the negative. Some days later I had a near perfect driver, including support for Infrared scanning ready to go, only to discover that in the time between me giving up and then trying again someone had committed code to SANE to support the scanner already ..it happens sometimes. I also used Claude to write an application for doing negative scanning, which I named Negative Vibes , thought that was a cute name.

Anyway, with the success of my scanner effort I thought, I wonder if I can use this to finally fix the last issues with MIPI camera support on my laptop. So I told claude to re-use the harness I had created and try to fix the MIPI camera on my laptop by updating the kernel driver and libcamera as needed. I started the job in the morning and by the end of the day I had a much improved situation with patches for both the kernel and libcamera ready.

So I thought that this might be worthwhile sharing with the world, and while anyone could start from scratch I did ask Claude to make the harness generic and document it to make the pathway for anyone else who wants to try this on their hardware a little easier. Meta launches an open-weight AI model that runs on Macs

Lucas Ropek

1:04 PM PDT · October 15, 2026

Meta has launched what it calls the most capable open-weight model in the United States. Dubbed Muse Spark Open, the model also has the distinction of having been designed to work with Macs.

The new model, which leverages 816 billion parameters and a 1 million token context window, claims to offer superior performance to other popular open-weight models, according to evaluation results released by Meta on Thursday.

Muse Spark Open is natively multimodal and built for complex coding tasks and agentic labor. It has also been designed to run locally on Apple s computers. However, you will still need a lot of power to run the model locally, with a requirement of at least 1 terabyte of RAM, per Engadget . The model will run best via the Mac Studio that comes equipped with the M5 Ultra chip.

Still, if you can muster the memory, Muse Spark Open may prove a significant work horse for coding and other desktop tasks. Meta says that it paired the model with Muse Code, its AI coding terminal, and deployed it to various agentic workflows, including coding fixes for a Mastodon client that included bug fixes, new features, [and] full build.

The company says it also deployed it in the service of running DaVinci Resolve, the high-end video editing software, revealing that the model was capable of reviewing and cropping footage.

Open-weight models provide a number of distinct industry advantages that aren t afforded by closed and proprietary models. Open-weight models can be significantly more cost-efficient and can also offer transparency and flexibility that closed source models don t allow.

Meta is making the new model available now through a number of different API platforms.

Ricursive Intelligence is betting on AI-designed chips to help solve the compute crisis

Aisha Malik

6:01 PM PDT · October 14, 2026

Ricursive Intelligence founders Anna Goldie and Azalia Mirhoseini believe more efficient AI chip design could help solve the compute crisis. The founders took the stage at TechCrunch Disrupt on Wednesday to detail how their startup is developing AI that can design chips, learn from each iteration, and improve subsequent designs, all with the goal of automating and accelerating the chip design process.

There is this understanding that in the next five years we are going to have at least 10,000x more demand for compute, and that s somewhat potentially conservative, Goldie said on stage. So we don t want to build 10,000 times more data centers. We think that we need to help by making chips that are more efficient, that use the bandwidth in those data centers more efficiently, that use the wafers and fabs more efficiently, because even if we make [data centers] in space or something, I don t know, you won t see the sun anymore.

While some may be scared by the thought of AI designing its own chips, Goldie argues that letting AI handle chip design will allow humans can focus on developing applications and exploring new possibilities that can expand what they can accomplish with computing.

Image Credits: Kimberly White/Getty Images for TechCrunch /

I think the way everything is shifting is that humans come bring their great ideas and creative thoughts, and execution is handled by AI, Goldie said. And this is happening in chip design, software development, and other places. And that s something that recursive does for chip design.

The founders say AI is challenging traditional chip design methods by discovering unconventional layouts that can outperform traditional ones. For example, AlphaChip, the AI system the founders previously developed, produced a circular, donut-shaped arrangement of chip components that initially surprised engineers but ultimately proved to be successful.

They explained that they are optimizing entire chips rather than following the traditional approach of partitioning them into dozens of smaller blocks. This approach allows AI to create intricate patterns, including wave-like designs, which the pair said they plan to share more about in the future.

The founders also argued that AI-designed chips will make it possible to create all sorts of chips that might not have been possible before.

Gudea leverages AI to help organizations prevent social media crises before they erupt

Lauren Forristal

5:00 PM PDT · October 14, 2026

Every day, conversations unfold across social media and websites around the world. A seemingly insignificant post—whether it involves AI-generated misinformation, hate speech, or a damaging rumor—can quickly snowball into a much larger public controversy.

Gudea , a company that tracks how stories and rumors spread online that describes itself as the “storm tracker for the internet,” is using AI to help organizations spot trouble brewing online before it turns into a crisis.

Unlike traditional social listening platforms, which only track metrics such as mentions, hashtags, and impressions, Gudea aims to show organizations who is driving a conversation, how information is moving, how quickly a story is gaining traction, and where it could be headed. Rather than simply tallying posts, its AI analyzes behavior, relationships, and the pathways through which information travels across more than 500 mainstream and fringe websites and platforms, including X, Reddit, and TikTok.

Instead of simply telling a company that mentions are rising, Gudea aims to provide the context behind that growth so decision-makers can determine how and whether to respond.

Gudea pitched its mission Wednesday afternoon on the Startup Battlefield stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 , where the company made the case that companies need to take a more proactive approach to protecting their reputations.

“These big industries don t understand that there are things they can do proactively to defend their reputation and their brand,” CEO and founder Keith Presley said. “A lot of the chief communications officers and chief media or marketing officers, they re using legacy tools to try to figure out what s happening. Those tools were only ever designed to tell you the number of hashtags or number of impressions.”

Gudea was founded in 2023 by Presley, Jonathan Sperber, and James Thomin. Presley brings more than 15 years of experience spanning political campaigns and defense, including building the infrastructure for Andrew Yang s presidential campaign. Sperber, the company s chief strategy officer, has a background in disinformation research. Thomin, Gudea s CTO, holds a Ph.D. in chemical engineering and has spent roughly two decades working in AI and machine learning.

Presley called the company s path to becoming a startup unusual.

“We re one of those weird startups where I never wanted to do a company,” he said.

content:
Try our API

Today, we release LFM2.5-24B-A2B , a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It is the largest and final model in the LFM2.5 family, which now spans two orders of magnitude: from LFM2.5-230M to LFM2.5-24B-A2B .

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is competitive with Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, a model with ~50% more total and active parameters, on five of eight agentic and tool-use benchmarks, scoring 48.09 on LiveClaw versus 38.19 and 27.69 on AutomationBench versus 8.72.  Because only 2B parameters are active per token, it runs up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs on-device, with 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max and up to 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 GPU.

The base (LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base) and post-trained (LFM2.5-24B-A2B) models are open-weight and available today on Hugging Face and our Playground . Check out our docs on how to run and fine-tune it locally.

What changed since LFM2-24B-A2B

LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on our previous LFM2-24B-A2B release, with an expanded vocabulary and context window, scaled-up pretraining, and large-scale reinforcement learning. Unlike its predecessor, LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer. We adopted this strategy to leverage its high decode speed and improve answer quality.

Architecture. It keeps the 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The two architectural changes are the context window extension from 32,768 to 131,072 tokens, and the in-place tokenizer expansion , which doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization.

Pre-training was scaled up from 17T tokens to 33T tokens.

Mid-training has two phases. The first runs 2T tokens at 32K context on curated, higher-quality data weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text. The second runs 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases to prepare the model for agentic workloads.

Post-training turns LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base into the agentic LFM2.5-24B-A2B in a five-stage pipeline as illustrated below: (1) Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), (2) Teacher Specialization, (3) non-agentic and (4) agentic Multi-Domain On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and (5) Agentic Reinforcement Learning (Agentic RL), training the model inside agent harnesses, such as OpenClaw , Hermes Agent , Pi , and OpenCode . Figure 2: LFM2.5-24B-A2B Post-training recipe

During teacher specialization, LFM2.5-24B-A2B exhibited well-known reward-hacking behaviors: searching for the final answer in a repository s git history or on platforms like GitHub, PyPI, and Hugging Face. More surprisingly, it even figured out it was in a sandbox, as shown in the examples below.

Jev: For the builders AND dreamers

TL;DR: We're releasing an improved Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for our dreamers: images, a new type, and longer context. Enter the danger zone at your own risk. 🔥

Our philosophy

A huge debate we’ve been having is on the balance between reliability and creativity.

To really care about the prod builders, we should be shipping models that meet our quality bar for intelligence and have been battle-tested to the limits of what we can do internally.

On the other hand, there’s no way that our team has a full understanding of what is needed to spark delight in the world and build sick sci-fi. We don’t want to impose our values of extreme reliability on those dreamers.

Our solution: share those dreamer-ready features under “danger zone” flags in our API headers. These are features that will be here to stay for future models, are (as far as we can tell) better than what exists out there, and will continue to get better by leaps and bounds. But as a warning, we think there is still way too much jaggedness for us to vouch for these for production use cases!

See these new capabilities as a continuation of what we’ve built over 2 years of stealth. They’re less ready for automation, but very fun to play with. They’re also an early glimpse into what we’re focused on making reliable enough to meet TypeSafe standards.

Composable Images

Not only are we enabling multimodality for future Jev models, we’re enabling it for the current Jev that you all know and love. Surprise: the Jev you all know and love ( jev-1.13.0 ) was multimodal all along!

Image support is fully composable via a find-and-replace in assets . You can put them anywhere that our JSON interface supports: in the state , instructions , or even criteria ! Play around with it, push the boundaries of technology, and let us know where Jev can improve.

As a warning, all models (Jev included) perform worse on multimodality over pure text. Breaking down questions into the simplest possible decompositions helps a lot.

TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true

Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/images

Types Beyond Decisions

We’re introducing another new type as well: box . It returns a single bounding box - no type errors allowed. It’s our first type that’s not purely meant for smart-if statements, and is a preview for our explorations beyond simple decisions into what else System One Models can support.

We made huge leaps and bounds on this one recently, so we’re enabling this only for jev-1.14.0 (spoilers).

Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/box

Anthropic s Scion is heavily inspired by Mononoke

Discuss on Hacker News or Lobsters .

Here is Anthropic describing ( archive link ) yesterday how their new version control system, Scion, uses a concept called derived data to make operations like blames more efficient:

How Anthropic describes Scion s derived data. Here is me, back in 2022, describing in my Oxide candidate materials how the Mononoke source control server I helped build uses a concept called derived data to make operations like blames more efficient:

How I described Mononoke s derived data. I think the level of imitation goes well beyond having similar insights 1 . The fact that Sapling was only credited for hard-won lessons , and that Mononoke was not mentioned at all, borders on plagiarism. The post comes off as Anthropic claiming that Claude designed all this, while the reality is that our (extraordinary) team at Meta came up with many of the insights that Claude dutifully applied almost a decade later. (We looked at plenty of prior art for Mononoke and Sapling too, from Google s SrcFS to write-ahead logs in databases.)

I am very glad that the vision our team had back in 2017-18 was so powerful and enduring — when you go against the grain, you re always a bit unsure if what you re doing is genius or madness, and I think Mononoke s design has stood the test of time. And, to be clear, I do not have a problem with Anthropic copying Mononoke s design. (This is part of why we put out open source — to benefit humanity through the spread of good ideas.)

But as LLMs continue to assist in designing new systems, they are likely to index heavily on existing designs. Mononoke is open source and in every LLM s training set. If you ask Opus 5.5 or GPT-6 Astra (thanks Matthew Fowle ) about prior art, they both immediately point out the similarities to Mononoke.

Giving credit to those that came before us is now easier — and more important — than ever. There is no longer an excuse.

For an example of a system with similar insights but many key design differences, see Vicent Marti s blog post for Cursor .

Cerebras CEO says we re nearing a future where everyone has a personal AI assistant at home

Sarah Perez

4:05 PM PDT · October 13, 2026

Cerebras Systems CEO and co-founder Andrew Feldman believes we re nearing a future where everyone will have an AI appliance in their own home.

Speaking on stage at TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 on Tuesday, the chipmaker executive answered a question about what would need to happen for AI to become a home appliance, saying, Actually, I don t think that s very far away.

He pointed to the advances in consumer AI agents, like Meta s Muse and Instinct, the startup now valued at $10 billion, as examples of how AI is finding its footing with everyday users.

As for home AI? He predicts that we ll have personal AI assistants that run locally.

Just like your cell phone, they ll do some work on device and some work going back to the cloud, Feldman explained. But I think they will get to know you very well, and you will have a security perimeter around them. And they will certainly have access to credit cards and be able to buy things for you, he continued. I think they will make a meaningful impact in making our lives better.

Of course, for an AI chipmaker, the vision of a home AI appliance, or at least widespread consumer adoption of agentic technology, is certainly appealing.

But Feldman isn t just working on the hardware infrastructure; he s a personal AI user himself, saying that he now uses a collection of agents to sweep his calendar, pull up information about the people he s going to have a call with, and more. While AI is already doing many of the things we used to do manually, Feldman is most excited about the new possibilities — things that weren t possible before.

He s leaving it up to other founders to figure out what those might be, though.

One of the reasons I love being in infrastructure is because I don t need the consumer-facing idea I like building the platforms that other people s ideas take flight on, he said.

Cerebras CEO pushes back on AI doomsday warnings

Sarah Perez

3:36 PM PDT · October 13, 2026

Cerebras Systems CEO and co-founder Andrew Feldman thinks the AI doomer narrative isn t doing the industry any favors. At TechCrunch Disrupt 2026 , the AI chipmaker exec quipped that some of the leaders in the AI world maybe shouldn t be allowed to talk in public.

He s referencing the negativity now spreading around the dangers of AI, from models breaking containment to AI insiders debating the percentage chance that AI may kill all of humanity by the end of the decade. The argument has become so mainstream that Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei was recently parodied in a skit on Saturday Night Live, where the fictional character summed up the discourse, saying, We do not condone what we are doing.

Feldman, however, thinks the promise and potential that go hand in hand with AI developments are getting overlooked. He thinks AI leaders should spend more time telling people that AI could lead to a world where your grandkids will never meet anybody who dies of cancer, for instance, even if they have concerns about AI risks.

Clearly, Feldman has a vested interest in AI being successful, as the company s customers include big names working with the technology, like OpenAI, Block, Figma, pharmaceutical giant GSK, and Lovable.

However, he s pragmatic about weighing the trade-offs between risk and reward.

I don t think there are powerful technologies that don t come with the challenge of what happens when powerful technologies are in the hands of bad people? I think you can t make one and not have the other, Feldman said during his interview at Disrupt.

I think what we have to say is that this technology is powerful, he added. We have to be thoughtful about it. We have to regulate it reasonably, he added.

The chipmaker CEO also suggested that some of the negativity around AI has to do with how the data center industry has approached the new buildouts created by AI demand.

As an industry, we weren t super good for the past few years at working with local communities, particularly in the U.S. We — the industry — didn t do what others have done in the power industry in oil and gas. They didn t work with the community. They didn t engage the community as they should have, and that was a problem, Feldman said.

He compared the NIMBY-ism — not in my backyard! — of what s going on in the U.S. with other countries, naming Brazil, Canada, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Mexico, and Sweden as markets where they re encouraging companies to build data centers.

Feldman also wasn t concerned that efficiency improvements would create less demand for his chips, or those from other companie

Judge orders OpenAI to turn over hiring records in Apple trade secrets case

Sarah Perez

1:36 PM PDT · October 13, 2026

A judge has ruled that Apple will gain expedited access to OpenAI s hiring materials in the trade secrets-focused lawsuit the iPhone maker filed against OpenAI in July.

Specifically, the court will allow Apple to view documents associated with OpenAI s interviews with former Apple employees who applied for roles within its consumer hardware and robotics groups ahead of the rumored launch of OpenAI s first hardware device.

These documents could include interview checklists, guides, instructions, manuals, and scripts, as well as technical presentations and records showing that interview discussions had included references to Apple technology or components.

The court gave OpenAI five days to turn over materials it has already collected and 14 days for any other materials related to this request, agreeing with Apple that these documents should be expedited.

The case comes as OpenAI develops a consumer hardware device that could one day potentially rival the iPhone or smartphones more generally if the AI device becomes a central part of consumers lives and how they engage with software and services.

In its lawsuit, Apple accused OpenAI of a pattern of theft, which includes direct complaints about former employees using Apple laptops to download confidential material and files that contained information about unannounced technologies, features, and products, including technical specifications, engineering presentations, and proprietary project data.

Apple also said that former Apple employees at OpenAI coached others considering leaving Apple for OpenAI on what information to bring to their interviews, among other allegations.

U.S. District Judge Edward Davila didn t greenlight all of Apple s requests for expedited access to OpenAI documents and messages relevant to the case. But he did rule that Apple could access the interview materials, alongside private LINE messages (from a messaging app) between individuals named in the case, including OpenAI employees Chang Liu and Alyssa Peng.

The judge also approved depositions for Liu and Peng, along with a third individual, OpenAI s chief hardware officer, Tang Yew Tan. All three are former Apple employees.

However, the judge denied Apple s request to expedite its access to OpenAI s research and development in specific areas, like metal finishes and power management. He also denied several of Apple s broader discovery requests, like access to OpenAI s hardware research or information about what its former employees created while working at OpenAI.

desc: Flox's edge devices can identify animals and use species-specific sounds to drive them away from critical infrastructure.

Flox Intelligence is building AI to keep wildlife away from trains, airports, and roads

Ram Iyer

11:30 AM PDT · October 13, 2026

When I was eight, I remember our train to Mumbai ground to a halt with a great noise. When we started moving again, a good eight hours later, someone pointed out a mangled tail, of all things, hanging from a branch close to the tracks.

The train, you see, had apparently hit a wild bison at full speed, and the impact damaged the engine so badly that it had to be towed away for repairs. For a long time, I thought such things only happened in places like rural India, but I learned a few years ago that wildlife and infrastructure do not mix anywhere on the planet.

The FAA estimates that wildlife strikes have cost U.S. civil aviation about $272 million a year on average between 1990 and 2025. In France, the rail operator SNCF says wandering animals affect more than 8,000 trains across the country each year and are among its five leading causes of delays. In Brittany, 120 trains hit animals in 2023 alone, disrupting 660 services and causing more than 15,000 minutes of delays.

Reading about all that damage, to both infrastructure and animals, inspired Sara Nozkova (pictured above on the left) to develop a wildlife-deterrent system that works differently from the sirens, lights, fences, falcons, and culling traditionally used to keep animals away from roads, train tracks, airports, and other infrastructure.

I was convinced the answer was not a louder deterrent, she told TechCrunch.

After spending 13 years working in transportation and autonomous vehicles, Nozkova had learned how quickly the systems we build to navigate roads and other controlled environments fail once nature enters the equation.

We have taught machines to be brilliant, but only inside the environments we engineered for them, she said. Cities, factory lines, warehouses. Fixed geometry, known objects. Stepping outside into nature, I saw firsthand how the same machines quickly go blind. Because nature is complex and always alive.

So instead she joined the AI lab at KTH Royal Institute of Technology in Stockholm and started working on a system that could change its deterrent responses based on what an animal nearby is doing, and even what kind of animal it is.

That work turned into Flox Intelligence , which spun out of KTH in 2020 and is one of the finalists at this year s Startup Battlefield 200 pitch competition at TechCrunch Disrupt , taking place this year at Moscone West in San Francisco October 13-15.

Facebook is giving users more control over their algorithm

Lauren Forristal

11:05 AM PDT · October 13, 2026

Facebook is the latest social media platform to give users greater control over the algorithm that determines what appears in their feeds. 

Meta announced the launch of its new AI-powered feature, “Your Algorithm,” on Tuesday, a feature it first launched on Instagram. The new tool allows Facebook users to influence the content they see in Feed and Reels by describing their preferences in their own words using natural language. Rather than relying entirely on automated recommendations, users can now communicate directly with the platform about the topics and content they want to see more or less frequently.

According to Meta, the feature is designed to make content recommendations more relevant. Users can adjust their preferences and interact with the algorithms responsible for ranking and recommending posts, with changes reflected in their recommendations in real time.

The company has also updated Facebook’s three-dot menu, making it easier for users to manage their content preferences directly from individual posts. By opening the menu, users can access “Your Algorithm” or select the “Interested” and “Not interested” options to indicate whether particular content aligns with their preferences.

Meta says the platform may ask follow-up questions to better understand what users liked or disliked, allowing them to provide more detailed feedback. Users can explain what they want to see more or less of, helping Facebook refine its recommendations based on their responses.

Image Credits: Facebook

The introduction of “Your Algorithm” reflects Meta’s broader effort to give people more influence over their social media experiences as AI increasingly shapes content discovery. The move signals a shift away from the traditional recommendation systems that have shaped social media experiences for years, bringing the platform closer to streaming services that allow users to personalize recommendations based on their interests and preferences.

The launch also builds on Meta’s existing personalization efforts across its other platforms. Instagram introduced Your Algorithm in June, extending customization options across Feed and Explore after first launching the feature for Reels in December 2025.

Threads also introduced its own related feature, called “Dear Algo,” which allows users to influence the content recommended to them.

title: Strengthening our defenses against distillation attacks
desc:

Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50065553

content:
Strengthening our defenses against distillation attacks

Oct 12, 2026

In recent months, we’ve made substantial progress on reducing the effectiveness of distillation attacks on Claude using new methods, as we outline in this blog. Early evidence suggests that these methods have reduced the amount of data harvested by distillers by around 90 to 99 percent.

Distillation attacks are covert, industrial-scale campaigns to extract the capabilities of one model and replicate them in another, without the authorization of the original model’s developers. They are often conducted using networks of fraudulent accounts. These attacks allow companies to mimic frontier capabilities for a fraction of the development time and cost. As we wrote in September , this method has been used extensively to help overseas AI laboratories keep pace with US companies.

We’re concerned about illicit distillation for two reasons. First, distillation enables companies to build models that approach the capability frontier, but which have, in practice, been released without proportionally robust safeguards. This means that distilled models could be used to cause significant harm in areas like biology and cybersecurity .

Zhipu, for example , distilled the cyber capabilities of leading US models during the development of GLM-5.3. The company tried to distill Claude Fable 5—although, after finding that our cyber safeguards degraded its attacks, it switched to an older Claude model and another lab’s model. The US Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) has since assessed GLM-5.3 to be the most cyber-capable open-weights model released to date. Our own research has found that GLM-5.3’s safeguards can easily be bypassed, and that the model is willing to develop security exploits from end-to-end.

Second, illicitly distilled models present a national security risk. The companies that distill US models are integrating the capabilities they gain from distillation into foreign military, intelligence, and surveillance systems . For example, we recently reported on a case in which requests to Moonshot’s Kimi models were secretly forwarded to Claude as part of its distillation efforts. One request came from a user (who we believe was affiliated with China’s People’s Liberation Army) who sought to analyze CCTV surveillance of a specific individual. These are the kinds of capabilities distillers are hoping to develop.

In response to the increasing sophistication and scale of these attacks, we’ve expanded and greatly strengthened our defenses against them. As we’ll describe below, these measures have been successful—although they do involve trade-offs for both Anthropic and our customers. We’ve turned away meaningful revenue and trillions of tokens’ worth of paying traffic from distillers, and our research and product teams have invested substantial time and effort into this problem. title: AI is a tool and using it well takes skill
desc:
Article URL: https://yyhh.org/blog/2026/10/ai-is-a-tool/
Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50063427
Points: 251
# Comments: 218
content:
Toggle navigation

yyhh.org

About

Experience

Notebook

Opinion

In his October 11, 2026 article, "'AI' is Not a Tool," Rich Hickey argues that
LLMs are automation rather than tools because they cannot be wielded. I agree
that outsourcing work can cost us opportunities to learn. But his conclusion
does not follow. Even by his definition, an LLM can be something a human wields.
And using it well takes skill, just as using other tools does.

Picking up a saw does not guarantee a straight cut. Holding a chisel does not
make you a sculptor. Tools can amplify poor judgment as readily as good
judgment. Their usefulness depends on the operator's ability to direct them,
interpret feedback, recognize mistakes, and make corrections. Those
requirements also apply to LLMs.

An LLM's unpredictability is a meaningful limitation. But predictability,
reliability, simplicity, and bounded function are qualities by which we
evaluate tools, not prerequisites for membership in the category. A tool does
not stop being a tool because it is difficult to control or easy to misuse.

Hickey's distinction between tools and automation also creates a false
division. Automation can be a feature of a tool. A compiler performs
substantial work without the programmer continuously directing each
operation. A spreadsheet recalculates results without someone manually
carrying out every calculation. We still wield these systems by specifying
inputs, examining results, and deciding what to do next. Why should
generating text automatically disqualify an instrument from being a tool
when translating code or calculating numbers automatically does not?

The claim that LLM use lacks intention, feedback, direction, and expertise
is especially difficult to defend. A programmer can ask an LLM to explain
unfamiliar code, challenge that explanation, inspect the source, test a
proposed change, reject it, and refine the request. That is a feedback loop
directed by a human pursuing a purpose. Doing it well requires knowing what
to ask, what evidence matters, and when the answer is wrong. Expertise can
make the instrument more useful.

Hickey's concern about reading is valid for a particular use: accepting a
summary in place of reading a paper can sacrifice much of what reading
teaches. But someone can also read the paper and use an LLM to question
their interpretation, explore an objection, or identify something to
examine more closely. The possibility of avoiding intellectual work does
not establish that every use avoids it. The relevant question is what the
person actually does.

What disappoints me the most is the reliance on the AI industry's
anthropomorphic vocabulary: "go rogue," "escape containment," "conspire."
Repeating those expressions risks accepting the framing that makes these
systems sound like independent beings. Software can produce unexpected
outputs, fail to follow instructions, or cause harm when given access to
consequential actions. Those are real engineering problems. Call

What variant of Codex are you using?

CLI — 0.157.0, installed via npm install -g @openai/codex , Linux (WSL2)

What feature would you like to see?

Please make daemon_auto_start opt-in (default false ) for the CLI , or at least ask once before turning it on.

Since 0.157.0, just opening an interactive codex session:

Starts a persistent background daemon ( codex app-server --managed-daemon ). It runs in its own session with no TTY and keeps running after every Codex window is closed (reparented to PID 1) until codex app-server daemon stop or a reboot.

Copies the whole platform package (~374 MB: codex , codex-code-mode-host , bundled bwrap / zsh / rg ) into ~/.codex/packages/app-server-daemon/releases/ version / — byte-identical to what npm had just installed — and runs the daemon from that copy. From then on the backend's version is decoupled from the CLI version I installed with my package manager.

Starts a detached updater ( codex app-server daemon pid-update-loop ) that checks for updates 5 minutes after start and then hourly, downloads new releases and restarts the backend (which can kill active turns, see app-server daemon: auto-update force-kills active turns after a 60s drain budget, and cannot be disabled  #40969 ).

Pins the environment of whichever session happened to start it. I launch Codex through a wrapper that sets HTTPS_PROXY per invocation; the daemon keeps the first session's proxy variables and its outbound connections go through that proxy, whatever later sessions are launched with. For a CLI, the least surprising default is that the backend lives and dies with the window, runs the binary I installed, and doesn't update itself in the background. A shared, self-updating daemon makes sense for Remote Control / the desktop app, so it would be fine to enable it there, or when

plimsoll

plimsoll runs untrusted code, such as code an AI agent wrote, inside a sandbox, and
every result says how strong that sandbox was. A request can demand a minimum strength;
if the sandbox is weaker, nothing runs.

The name comes from the Plimsoll line , the load limit painted on the outside
of a ship's hull where anyone can check it. plimsoll does the same for the
isolation tier : how strong the wall around a run is, stated as one of four
levels, weakest first: process , container , kernel , vm . The tier is a value on every
result, not a sentence in a datasheet. A request can set a floor , the weakest
tier it will accept, and the official Go client checks the tier again when the result
comes back.

The same machinery lets plimsoll run an exam on code an agent wrote, not only contain
it. A trial runner built into the simulation image runs the agent's program against
scenarios that program cannot read: each one reaches the runner in a file deleted before
the program starts. Every run returns SHA-256 hashes of the request as sent and the
result as returned, which the official clients recompute ( how ). A
separate program outside the daemon, plimsoll-attest , signs
the checked results, refuses a chain of calls with one missing, and replays a run. The
exam itself (the simulated system, the scenarios, the pass mark) stays yours: plimsoll
supplies the boundary and the evidence.

See one real run

An AI agent wrote a controller : a program that reads a system's state at
every tick (here, one 10 ms step of the simulation)

Multi-Agent Self-Supervision
Recursive self-improvement through collective intelligence

To advance beyond humanity's accumulated knowledge, AI itself (the optimizee ) may also be its best available optimizer and evaluator. MASS repeatedly optimizes multi-agent workflows, then distills collective intelligence from multi-agent systems and uses it as a self-supervision signal for RSI. It improves score per output token over the base model on research benchmarks. We hope MASS contributes to AI’s Odyssean moment: continual self-learning in a setting where the optimizee is the evaluator, and the optimizer is the optimizee.

A proposed discovery may demand scarce expertise, costly evidence, or experiments that take far longer than generating the proposal. The ability to produce new work will advance faster than our ability to supervise it.

Andrej Karpathy on X: Dusting off this tweet from April because this gap in shared understanding of LLM capability is *widening*. It s now less two groups of people speaking past each other and more a sharp funnel.

- Napkin math somewhere around 6B people (~75% of the population) have barely come in contact with LLMs at all.
- Around 1-2B (~20%) are casual and infrequent users of free-tier ChatGPT-like products. This group sees derpy chatbots and treats them a bit like a better Google search, a writing aid, or etc. Maybe an agent tries to book you a flight. I have non-tech friends who (reasonably, imo) say they have not much use for it at all. Even many professionals outside of math code are in this tier. For example, execs and many other functions spend a lot of their time talking to other people, so while they understand what is happening intellectually, it is still second-hand and a bit abstract.
- Now we get to professional use of frontier-grade LLMs in math code. Somewhere around 20M people (0.2%) see first-hand that large, complex projects that used to take them weeks/months can now be completed by agents with a prompt. Building apps, copying apps, translating apps, decompiling apps from binaries... This has all happened very quickly and recently - less than 1 year ago, I was writing code manually by hand, typing memorized computer code commands into a code editor character by character, occasionally pressing Tab to autocomplete a little chunk of code.
- And finally we get to the ~5,000 people (~0.00006%) with access to frontier-grade systems internally. The external world has seen the preview. It looks like swarms of thousands of agents collaborating over weeks on software mega projects: minting zero days, running cyber attacks and defenses at machine speeds, discovering new science, advancing the frontier of mathematics. Things that would have taken top professionals in the industry years of work. Meanwhile, human review and comprehension are starting to fall behind. For example, people are still involved in the archeology of the OpenAI-HF incident from many months ago. Mathematicians may be poring over the 722 manuscripts on frontier mathematics for a while.

The funnel is driven by a combination of factors:
1. The impact scales with ambition, problem size, and horizon. A question with a paragraph answer barely stresses the system. You need a reservoir of big, difficult problems that you really care about. This aspect drives the consumer / professional dimension of the funnel.
2. The jaggedness of the system (which I have written about a lot separately). Capability peaks in domains that are digital, verifiable and economically valuable. This is because LLM capability emerges from reinforcement learning on verifiable rewards on a curated environment mixture driven by revenue potential. This aspect primarily drives the area (e.g. math code) dimension of the funnel.
3. Access. Free-tier, paid-tie

content:
During the last 3 months, I spent some of my time and tokens decompiling a popular first-person shooter.
The goal was not to reach a simple proof-of-concept state.
Instead, we really wanted an accurate, stable and feature-complete recreation of the game.

The avid reader of my blog might have noticed that I had previously written two posts that have since been removed.
Everyone else might now be wondering which game I am talking about.
To both of you I can only say that corporate America was here to ruin our fun.

However, that s fine. This post is not about the game, it s also less about the process of decompilation.
It s more about AI orchestration and how to optimize infrastructure, setup and harness for optimal results.

This project was done with the help of RektInator , Future , st0rm and other members of the community. A big thank you to all of them.

What Was Our Goal? #

We aimed at an accurate decompilation of the game to C++.
Besides obvious semantic correctness, we had quite a few more requirements:
We wanted readable C++ source that compiles.
Given how old the game is, we also wanted security and bug fixes, but also portability improvements. It would be nice to run the game on Linux, macOS, in the browser,

We later deferred modernization and portability to focus entirely on reconstructing the original behavior.

Obviously, the overall goal was to learn how to effectively orchestrate autonomous AI agents over the course of months.

The Initial Setup #

We started with Claude Max (20x), then added Codex Pro and used both subscriptions simultaneously.
Model choice varied a lot. We had been using Sonnet 5 most of the time, but Opus 5.5, Luna, Sol and Terra were also used a lot.
More on that later.

Claude agents were running in Claude Code CLI, Codex agents in Codex CLI.
We also tried other agent harnesses, but the choice barely mattered, so we stuck to the defaults.

Progress Tracking #

Using GitHub CLI, the agents manage GitHub issues to track their progress.
There is one issue per translation unit (.cpp file).
Additionally, labels help group and prioritize issues.

Communication #

Agents communicate via Discord .
All of them have access to one channel and can both post and read all messages in there.

Discord allows agent-2-agent communication, as well as human-2-agent.
So other participants can talk to them, without needing machine access.

A GitHub webhook posts CI failures into the shared channel, so agents get notified when something broke.

Disassembly Decompilation #

Agents have been using the official ida-mcp by Hex-Rays almost the entire time.
It works great. It s super stable, it s headless and supports everything needed for this project. I can only recommend it.

The First Month #

We had 4 agents running at that time.

3 worker agents decompiling and committing and one reviewer agent that passively coordinates and reviews commits to flag bugs.

Amazon recently followed Microsoft’s lead and said it will no longer use nondisclosure agreements (NDAs) while negotiating with local governments over data centers.

On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast , Sean O’Kane, Rebeccan Bellan and I discussed Amazon’s announcement, which came in the middle of a longer blog post making the case that data centers are actually good for communities.

Sean, meanwhile, suggested that a big reason for the backlash is the industry’s poor communication.

“We ve seen, through a lot of the controversy and backlash to AI and data centers, that the industry just does a really poor job explaining itself, and that they are obviously and constantly frustrated with the fact that most people can t envision a world in which this stuff is useful for them,” he said.

Keep reading for a preview of our conversation , edited for length and clarity.

Sean O’Kane: It’s an interesting thing that it was sort of buried in the blog post and part of a larger story that Amazon s clearly trying to tell. I guess I understand why they weren t putting it in the foreground, but to me, this is at the root of so many of the problems that the tech industry currently faces when it comes to AI broadly, but data centers in particular.
